lines: A moment ago, one platform kept every one of its old storage blocks around forever, letting you reach into the past.
That one couldn't be run here at all -- only read about.
Here's a second platform, also unreachable, but built on an entirely different foundation underneath.
Picture one single system that both holds a table's bytes and crunches through a query against them.
Does that same system still do both of those jobs today, or did holding the bytes and crunching the query end up somewhere else entirely?
Guess before the next slide answers it.
answer: They ended up somewhere else entirely.
Holding the bytes and crunching the query now live on two separate systems.

lines: One system holds every byte on a shared, column-oriented storage layer, far away from any one query.
A completely different cluster, managed on its own, reads that storage over a dedicated internal network to actually run the query.
Neither side ever needs to touch local disks belonging to the other.
A table gets sliced into segments first, so a filter can throw out whole segments that can't possibly match.
Inside the segments that survive, rows get sorted into tighter blocks for the exact same kind of filter.
Two passes of the identical idea, each one narrowing what actually gets read.
Now picture a saved, precomputed answer to a question you ask over and over against a table that keeps changing underneath it.
Nobody sits there refreshing that saved answer by hand.
It just stays current on its own, quietly, every time the table underneath it shifts.
Skipping unneeded segments and reusing a precomputed answer both still mean one more query actually has to run.
Is there anything that skips running a frequently repeated question altogether, rather than just running it faster?
Guess before the next slide answers it.
answer: Yes, something skips running it altogether.
A caching layer sitting in front of the whole system catches it instead.

lines: That caching layer keeps the data behind your most frequent questions sitting ready in memory, in front of everything else.
Nothing about the question itself, or the table it reads from, ever has to change for that to kick in.
It's just faster the next time, without anyone asking for that.
Getting data in splits two different ways: one big delivery, dropped in all at once from outside storage.
Or a steady trickle, one row after another, arriving continuously instead.
Same destination table, two very different rhythms of arrival.
That steady trickle used to only promise it would probably get every row there, eventually, with no hard guarantee.
The newer version of that same trickle now tracks exactly where each writer left off.
That tracking is what finally turns probably into a guarantee: every row, exactly once.
One system held the bytes and ran the question itself, together -- now two separate systems split that job, joined by a network between them.
Narrowing by segment, narrowing again by block, catching repeats before they run, two different rhythms for getting data in -- every one of those rests on that same split.
A third platform is coming next, and it splits nothing at all -- its compute and its storage live on the very same machines.
